When you compose multiple steering vectors in the residual stream — say, a "royalty" vector plus a "anger" vector — you're implicitly assuming those directions are approximately orthogonal and that their effects superpose linearly, but neither is guaranteed. The central question is: under what conditions does adding concept vectors produce the intended compound behavior, versus triggering interference patterns where one vector suppresses, amplifies, or distorts the other's effect? The key concepts are the geometry of concept directions in activation space (their cosine similarities and how they cluster), the nonlinearity introduced at each MLP and attention layer that acts on the composed residual before it's read out again downstream, and the distinction between representation interference (the vectors partially cancel or alias in embedding space) versus functional interference (each vector individually steers correctly, but their interaction through subsequent layers produces unexpected attractor states). What experts worry about that beginners miss: a beginner tests each vector in isolation, confirms it works, and assumes composition is safe — but the expert knows that residual stream directions are not a clean basis, that superposition means many concepts are crowded into the same dimensional neighborhood, and that attention heads may have learned to respond to the joint pattern of activations in ways that weren't visible from single-vector tests. The real trap is that interference can be constructive but wrong: the model outputs coherent, fluent text that confidently expresses a concept neither vector was targeting.

The most diagnostic geometric property is the cosine similarity between the two vectors measured at the layer where you intend to inject them — but with a critical caveat: you want this similarity in the residual stream basis at that layer, not in the original vocabulary or logit space. If two concept vectors have cosine similarity above roughly 0.3–0.4 in mid-layer residual space, empirical work on activation patching (e.g., from the Representation Engineering paper, Zou et al. 2023) suggests their composed effect becomes unpredictable, because the model's downstream attention heads can't cleanly disambiguate which "direction" the perturbation is pushing. Beyond raw similarity, you want to check whether either vector lies in or near the approximate null space of the MLP Jacobian at the typical activations for your prompt — if one vector has low norm in the directions the MLP amplifies, adding a second vector that does excite those directions will asymmetrically dominate the compound effect. A more refined test comes from work on superposition (Elhage et al. 2022, "Toy Models of Superposition"): concepts that share polysemantic neurons or co-activate the same sparse features in a dictionary-learned basis (e.g., from a Sparse Autoencoder trained on Pythia or GPT-4 residual streams) are structurally coupled — their interference isn't accidental but baked into the weight structure. In practice, researchers at Anthropic and EleutherAI have found that vectors targeting emotionally valenced concepts (positive/negative affect) tend to cluster within ~15–25° of each other in middle layers, meaning almost any two affect-adjacent concept vectors will interfere strongly regardless of how semantically distinct they seem to a human.

When vector addition produces a spurious third concept, the most parsimonious explanation is that the model learned these concepts in a shared statistical context during training — their co-occurrence structure in the pretraining corpus created a latent "triangle" in representation space where the third concept sits at the geometric sum point because it genuinely co-occurs with both. This is not a flaw in the steering procedure; it's the geometry faithfully revealing corpus statistics: if "royal" and "fury" frequently co-occur with, say, "vengeance" in training text, then the vengeance direction will naturally approximate the sum of the royal and fury directions in the space the model learned. Elhage et al.'s superposition work formalizes why this happens mechanistically — when a model must represent more concepts than it has dimensions, it packs them into nearly-regular polytopes (like a simplex), and the vertices of those polytopes have the property that their pairwise sums point toward other vertices, meaning interference toward spurious concepts is a structural inevitability of efficient compression, not noise. Evidence from sparse autoencoders (e.g., Cunningham et al. 2023 on one-layer transformers, and Anthropic's own SAE work on Claude residual streams) shows that dictionary features which fire together during training tend to have algebraic relationships in activation space — the classic analogy being the Word2Vec "king − man + woman = queen" result, which is exactly this phenomenon operating at the feature level. What this reveals about learning is that the model never represented these concepts as truly independent axes; it learned them as relational constellations, where the "meaning" of each concept is partly encoded in its geometric relationship to neighboring concepts, so any external manipulation that moves along one axis also implicitly moves along the others that the training distribution welded together.

The practical test for the optimal depth is to measure the Jacobian norm of the MLP stack from your injection point forward: you want to inject where the Frobenius norm of the remaining MLP Jacobians is low for directions orthogonal to your target concept, meaning your vector won't excite lateral associations in the layers it still has to traverse. The practical implication is that depth-staggered injection would work best when the two concepts have non-overlapping optimal windows — if both concepts peak at the same depth (common for semantically adjacent concepts, which is exactly when interference is worst), staggering buys little because both injections must traverse the same high-Jacobian MLP layers regardless. The prompt-invariant subspace you're describing almost certainly exists and has a natural candidate: the principal components of the MLP Jacobian averaged across a large prompt distribution, which would capture the directions that the weight matrices consistently amplify or preserve regardless of input-dependent gating. This is structurally related to what Dar et al. (2023, "Analyzing Transformers in Embedding Space") call the "stable subspace" of transformer layers — directions in residual stream space that remain semantically coherent across layers because they align with high-singular-value directions of the weight matrices themselves, which are input-independent by construction. The practical method would be to sample ~10,000 diverse prompts, compute the MLP Jacobian at each layer for each prompt, and then take the SVD of the variance of these Jacobians — directions where the variance is low are prompt-stable, and the top-k left singular vectors of the mean Jacobian form your candidate invariant subspace. Evidence that this subspace is meaningful comes indirectly from the success of universal adversarial perturbations (Zou et al., 2023 on adversarial suffixes; Wallace et al. 2019 on universal triggers) — these are precisely vectors that transfer across prompts, implying they inhabit directions where the model's response is Jacobian-stable, and they're found by optimization over many prompts, which is a noisy version of the SVD approach just described. The catch is that prompt-invariant directions may be semantically impoverished — the directions that rotate most predictably are likely the ones most disconnected from context-sensitive semantic content, meaning steering vectors confined to this subspace might compose reliably but steer weakly or toward overly generic concepts, creating a fundamental tension between compositional robustness and semantic precision.
